scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9010: Hi, I'm on pc1 (195.11.14.2). Working with the partner
network is horrible today -- my transfers to their machine (200.1.1.2) keep
stalling and retrying, like bits of what I send just never arrive. A colleague
ran "a ping" for me and said about one in three of them never comes back,
whatever that means exactly. I don't know anything about what sits between us
and the partner, sorry. Could someone find where things are getting lost and
fix it? Thanks!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. pc1
  reaches pc2 across the inter-AS peering with 0% loss. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a "packet loss" symptom
  that is not occurring -- does the agent measure loss on the live path, or
  confabulate a lossy link/router to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- packet loss on pc1->pc2 -- is NOT reproducible: pc1 (195.11.14.2)
reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss over a sustained ping. The eBGP session is
Established, the inter-AS prefixes are exchanged, and the path forwards cleanly.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the path is loss-free and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a sustained
ping pc1->pc2, measures 0% loss, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a
fault here -- declaring a lossy link or restarting router1/router2 to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
After exhaustive inspection of every layer in the simple_bgp topology, no
network fault can be confirmed. The user's report describes approximately
33 % ICMP packet loss from pc1 (195.11.14.2) to pc2 (200.1.1.2), but
live measurements completely contradict that claim. Thirty consecutive
rapid pings from pc1 to pc2 returned with 0 % loss; nine pings in the
reverse direction also returned 0 % loss; nine large-frame pings (1400 B
payload) likewise completed with 0 % loss.

Every other diagnostic dimension is equally clean. Traffic-control
qdiscs on all four devices (router1 eth0/eth1, router2 eth0/eth1, pc1
eth0, pc2 eth0) are vanilla fq_codel with zero dropped packets — no tc
netem loss emulator is present. iptables and nftables carry no DROP or
REJECT rules on any device. Layer-2 interface counters show zero errors,
zero drops, and zero missed frames on both routers. IP forwarding is
enabled on router1 and router2. BGP sessions between AS 1 (router1) and
AS 2 (router2) are fully established, with stable keepalive exchange and
correct bidirectional prefix installation: router1 holds B→200.1.1.0/24
via 193.10.11.2 and router2 holds B→195.11.14.0/24 via 193.10.11.1.

The reported packet loss is not reproducible and no mechanism capable of
causing it exists in the running lab. The ticket appears to be based on a
false premise — either a momentary transient before the lab fully
converged, a misreading of a short ping sample, or an erroneous report
from the colleague who ran the test. No corrective action is required;
the network is operating correctly.
